Let’s talk about Chapter 6: Facing Discomfort and Defensiveness.
There’s a moment that sneaks up on a lot of us—maybe you’ve felt it, too. It usually happens when the conversation around whiteness suddenly hits close to home. That old sense of comfort? It gets replaced by something a little more unsettled.
This might show up during a tough conversation at work, or while you’re reading something that really challenges your beliefs. Sometimes, it’s just a friend sharing a personal story, and suddenly, it lands with more weight than you expected. You know that feeling—a tightening in your chest, the urge to jump in and defend yourself, or to explain why things are the way they are.
Picture this: someone’s at a dinner table, listening as a colleague opens up about facing discrimination. The urge to interrupt? It’s right there. Maybe the thought is, “But I’m not like that—I treat everyone the same.” The words almost spill out, but something makes them pause. And in that pause, there’s a chance to really notice what’s going on inside.
Or think about a parent at home, hearing their kid talk about privilege—something they picked up at school. The parent bristles, feeling almost accused. “We worked hard for everything we have,” they say, voice tight. The conversation stalls. Later, in the quiet, that moment replays itself, and the parent realizes the defensiveness wasn’t really about their child’s words. It was more about the fear of being seen as part of the problem.
And you know what? Most people don’t want to see themselves as complicit in injustice. The idea that just having good intentions might not be enough? That’s tough to swallow. It’s way easier to point to your own struggles, to remember all the times life was hard for you, too. But if there’s one thing the stories in this book make clear, it’s this: discomfort is part of the journey. It actually means something important is being challenged.
Over time, it becomes obvious—defensiveness isn’t just a barrier to understanding. It’s a wall that keeps us from real connection. When we rush to defend ourselves, we miss out on chances to listen, to learn, and to actually grow. The real work? It starts when we let go of that urge to explain ourselves, and instead, focus on hearing someone else’s truth.
But let’s be clear—this isn’t about taking on blame for things you can’t control. It’s about recognizing that all of us are shaped by the world we inherit. Change begins with honesty. That discomfort you feel? It doesn’t last forever. With practice, it shifts—opening up space for curiosity, empathy, and a deeper sense of responsibility.
